cards.title: Start Google Ads with Search and Shopping, add Performance Max later
cards.summary: Sequence Google Ads campaign types for an ecommerce store by beginning with intuitive Search and Shopping campaigns and only layering in Performance Max once the account holds enough purchase data.
cards.use_when: Deciding which Google Ads campaign types to launch first for a store, or judging whether the account is ready for Performance Max.
steps: Launch with Search (text ads) and Shopping (product carousel showing image, price point and click-through) because they are the most intuitive and easiest to understand, and they map to how people already think about Google ads: someone searches, relevant ads appear.

Hold off on Performance Max, Demand Gen and Display at the start; Performance Max draws on search, shopping, YouTube, Display, Discover and Gmail placements and relies heavily on Google's automatic targeting, bidding and placement, so it needs a lot of conversion data to work.

Treat roughly 100 purchases in the ad account as the point where adding a Performance Max campaign can work well (the source says 'more than say 100 purchases, ideally as many as possible'); this is a practitioner heuristic, not a hard rule.
Use the early Search/Shopping period to learn the platform and build conversion history before handing more control to automation.
If you already run Performance Max and results are murky, consider whether conversion volume is the issue before blaming the campaign type.
Verify current campaign-type names and setup screens in the Google Ads interface, since formats and options change.
caveats: The 100-purchase threshold is the presenter's rule of thumb for their own agency, not a published Google benchmark.
Performance Max can be added 'later on' as an addition rather than a replacement; the source does not say to abandon Search or Shopping.

cards.title: Concentrate cold-traffic spend on one or a few winning products
cards.summary: Focus Google Ads budget on the small number of SKUs that acquire cold-audience customers cheaply instead of spreading spend thinly across the whole catalog.
cards.use_when: Structuring Google Ads campaigns and budget allocation across a multi-SKU catalog, especially when prospecting to cold audiences.
steps: Audit the account for cost per purchase and ROAS by product; identify the one product or handful of products that acquire customers far more efficiently than the rest.

Divert budget away from the long tail of SKUs and into those winners rather than running broad campaigns across the full catalog — the source describes this as one of the fastest early wins when taking over an ecommerce account.
In hobby or enthusiast niches, expect the beginner/entry-level version of the product to be the cold-traffic hero, with advanced products sold later once the customer is invested.
Accept that in most ecommerce categories (the source cites apparel as an example) there is nearly always one item or product range that dominates cold-audience acquisition.
Segregate cold and warm strategy: keep cold traffic tightly focused, and reverse the logic for warm audiences.
Be prepared to re-engineer supply chain if one product suddenly sells far more than before — the source flags this as a real consequence ecommerce owners should anticipate.
caveats: The source is explicit that this focus applies to cold audiences only; remarketing can and should open up the full range.
Selling mostly one hero product may complicate eventually selling the business, though the source says that is not impossible at scale.

cards.title: Open up the full catalog only for warm and remarketing audiences
cards.summary: Use dynamic product catalog ads and remarketing to show warm visitors the exact products they engaged with, while selling the wider range to people already in the ecosystem.
cards.use_when: Building Google Ads remarketing and dynamic product ad campaigns for site visitors and past customers, or deciding which SKUs to show which audience.
steps: For warm audiences — especially previous purchasers and recent site visitors — do not apply the cold-traffic 'focus on one hero' rule; instead broaden the product set.
Run dynamic product ads using a product catalog so that someone who viewed or added a specific item to cart sees that item, rather than the storewide bestseller that may not match their intent.
Let Google use signals such as prior product views, add-to-cart events and past similar purchases to tailor which product is served to each user.
Use remarketing, email and SMS together to sell the rest of the range to people already in the ecosystem, since acquisition cost on these audiences is far lower.
Keep cold prospecting concentrated so the algorithm receives clean conversion signals, then spend the warm budget on breadth and repeat purchase.
caveats: The source presents this as their standard practice, not a universal law; catalog ad availability and feed requirements should be verified in the current Google Ads interface.

cards.title: Know AOV, margin and LTV before setting an allowable CAC
cards.summary: Calculate the unit economics that determine what the store can afford to pay to acquire a customer, using AOV, gross margin and lifetime value together.
cards.use_when: Setting target CPA/ROAS for Google Ads, deciding whether a campaign can be profitable, or diagnosing why acquisition costs feel unaffordable.
steps: Establish average order value first; the source says an AOV over $100 makes profitable advertising much easier, and if you are below that, get as close to $100 as possible.

If your AOV sits around $40, look for structural ways to lift it — bundling multiple items, buy-one-for-you buy-one-as-a-gift offers, or adding complementary products — rather than accepting the ceiling.

Calculate gross profit margin on the order, not just the sale price: an AOV of $120 at a 10% gross margin yields only about $12 of gross profit per order, which is easily exceeded by acquisition cost.
Identify which individual products carry better margins and direct more advertising budget toward them.
Estimate customer lifetime value (total spend over the customer relationship) and use it to set the maximum allowable cost per purchase.
caveats: The '$100 AOV' and '10% margin' figures are illustrative examples from the presenter, not benchmarks for any specific category.
Margin and LTV figures must come from your own P&L and cohort data; the source gives no method for calculating LTV.

cards.title: Raise allowable acquisition cost by improving LTV rather than shaving CPA
cards.summary: Grow customer lifetime value to justify a far higher cost per acquisition, prioritising scale and repeat purchase over small percentage cuts to CPA.
cards.use_when: Setting CPC/CPA ceilings, deciding whether to run ads at a temporarily unprofitable ROAS, or prioritising between conversion-rate tweaks and retention improvements.
steps: Model the arithmetic: if first-purchase value is $100 and average lifetime value rises to $400, the maximum acceptable cost per purchase can rise from roughly $30 to roughly $120 — a 4x increase in affordable acquisition cost (the source's own worked example).

Prioritise LTV levers — repeat purchases, subscriptions, consumable ecosystems, post-purchase email and SMS — over chasing a 15–20% reduction in cost per purchase, which the source describes as the focus of many businesses but not of the biggest, most successful companies.

Consider the Starbucks illustration the source gives: a roughly $5.65 average order value alongside a very large lifetime value means the business can justify spending far more than a few dollars to acquire one customer; the source explicitly says not every business will match that, but the logic still applies.
Accept a lower ROAS when LTV justifies it: the source describes scaling even at a 1.5 ROAS after doubling LTV, or going down to around 1.2, because the LTV work has made those numbers affordable.
Recognise that scale compounds — more customers means a larger remarketing pool, email list and SMS list, and more participants for seasonal promotions like Black Friday or Christmas.
caveats: All numeric examples (four to five times LTV, $30 to $120 CPA, 1.5 and 1.2 ROAS) are the presenter's illustrative figures, not benchmarks.

Deliberately advertising at a loss depends on reliable LTV measurement and cash flow to fund the payback period; the source warns that the free-gift style of aggressive front-end spend must be done intelligently with cash flow in mind.

cards.title: Use a free-plus-shipping or generous front-end offer to acquire at scale
cards.summary: Apply reciprocity by giving a desirable entry product away for the cost of shipping, then monetise the natural follow-on purchases the customer will need.
cards.use_when: Designing a new-customer acquisition offer or entry-point product for cold Google Ads traffic.
steps: Choose a giveaway product that creates demand for your paid range rather than satisfying the need outright — the source's example is a free football to a family whose child is starting to play: the ball arrives, and boots, apparel and garden goals follow naturally.
Charge only the cost of shipping/postage so the offer is genuinely low-risk for the buyer while still covering fulfilment costs.
Check that the giveaway suits a market-entry moment — the source frames it as best for introducing people to a new type of product or a new category they haven't bought before.
Model cash flow carefully: front-loading cost of goods and shipping ahead of repeat revenue only works if the business can fund the gap and the entry product genuinely leads to follow-on purchases.
Expect the goodwill and the customer relationship to produce the return later, through the same ecosystem you would use for remarketing, email and SMS.
caveats: The source insists this must be done intelligently and with attention to cash flow; it is not a blanket recommendation.
It only works where the free item predictably leads to additional purchases — a giveaway that closes the need will not pay back.

cards.title: Discount tactically instead of defaulting to blanket sales
cards.summary: Preserve gross profit by targeting discounts at high-margin products or AOV thresholds rather than running deep storewide sales that trigger a race to the bottom.
cards.use_when: Planning seasonal promotions, Google Ads offer messaging, or a discount-led acquisition campaign.
steps: Analyse which products carry high enough margin to be discounted without destroying gross profit, and discount those rather than the whole catalog.
Consider giving an inexpensive free item with the purchase of a high-margin product instead of cutting the price of the main item.
Gate discounts behind an AOV threshold — for example 'spend over X and get 20% off' — mirroring the free-shipping threshold mechanic that exists to raise AOV.

If you position as premium or luxury, avoid straight discounts altogether; the source compares it to a fine-dining restaurant, where you would not expect a discount on the menu but would expect free extras such as wine advice or valet parking. Offer complimentary add-ons instead.
If your entire business model is being the cheapest or bulk provider, the source says to lean into that as your competitive advantage and discount accordingly.
Recognise that discounting volume without gross profit is not a win, even if units move.
caveats: The source is a fan of running sales and discounts and is not arguing against them — only against doing them without margin analysis.
The threshold mechanic is presented as a general AOV technique; the specific percentage and threshold must be set from your own economics.

cards.title: Mine customer reviews to write ad copy and find product fixes
cards.summary: Turn five-star review language into ad copy and creative, and use negative reviews to spot product and fulfilment problems.
cards.use_when: Writing Google Ads copy and creative for an ecommerce product, or looking for product/fulfilment improvements.
steps: Read reviews closely and identify repeated themes in five-star feedback — the source notes that owners often assume they know why people buy, but reviews frequently surface benefits they never considered important.
Amplify the recurring five-star themes directly in ad copy and creative, since ecommerce generates far more reviews than service businesses and the sample is large.
Use negative reviews as product feedback: the source's example is recurring packaging complaints, which can be fixed outside of marketing.

If you have no reviews yet, read competitor reviews: mirror what buyers praise about comparable products, and highlight any competitor weakness your product solves — for example a long installation time or slow delivery that you can guarantee against (the source uses a 24- or 48-hour guarantee as an illustration).
Make sure any claim you pull from reviews is true and verifiable for your own product before putting it in an ad.
caveats: The 24/48-hour delivery guarantee is the presenter's illustrative example of a competitive claim, not a promised result.
Review mining tells you what buyers say, not why non-buyers don't convert; pair it with other research.

cards.title: Fix the campaign before increasing budget — ROAS falls as spend rises
cards.summary: Scale only from a profitable position, because Google serves the best prospects first and return on ad spend declines as budgets grow.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise Google Ads budget on an underperforming campaign, or planning a scaling sequence for a store.
steps: If a campaign isn't profitable at the current budget, treat the problem as campaign quality — offer, ad copy, creative and targeting — not under-spending; the source states plainly that raising budget in this situation nearly always makes ROAS worse.

Accept the structure of the auction: at low spend Google reaches the keenest prospects; as spend rises it extends to progressively less interested audiences who need more convincing, so ROAS declines to some degree.

Get the campaign comfortably profitable at the current spend before scaling, then scale with the expectation that ROAS will fall — the source says the drop can be minor rather than dramatic, but it will happen.
Evaluate the trade-off in total profit, not ratio: the source prefers a 4x ROAS at $100,000/month over a 6x ROAS at $10,000/month because absolute profit and customer volume are larger.
Expect the ROAS floor you can accept to shift upward as LTV work matures — the source describes scaling at 1.5, or even down to 1.2, after doubling LTV.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated view, framed as correcting a common misconception among newer advertisers; it assumes you have reliable profit and LTV data.
The source warns that scaling incorrectly will wreck results and references a separate scaling strategy it does not detail here.

cards.title: Track cross-platform attribution before trusting platform-reported results
cards.summary: Maintain independent attribution across ad channels and organic traffic so you know where purchases actually originate before making budget decisions.
cards.use_when: Setting up measurement for a Google Ads programme that also runs other paid channels or earns organic traffic.
steps: Recognise the risk the source describes: running ads across multiple channels plus organic traffic without accurate attribution means you are 'flying blind' on which channel produced the lead or sale.
Implement a dedicated attribution/tracking tool (the source names Hyros, which they use for their own ads) so that lead and purchase sources are visible across Google Ads and organic results.
Use the cross-channel view to see exactly where a lead or sale came from before shifting budget between Google and other channels.

Note that the source's example use case is tracking which source produced a booked call for their agency; the ecommerce application is the equivalent — attributing purchases rather than calls, and reconciling platform-reported conversions against a single source of truth.
Verify current integrations and pricing of any attribution tool directly, as interfaces and features change.
caveats: The source is a promotional segment for Hyros; treat the tool name as the presenter's stated preference, not a comparative evaluation.
The source does not establish accuracy figures for any attribution method.

cards.title: Build founder visibility and tell the product origin story
cards.summary: Use a founder personal brand or, at minimum, the product's origin story as a trust asset that lifts Google Ads performance.
cards.use_when: Developing brand positioning and ad creative for an ecommerce store, or deciding whether to invest in founder-led content.
steps: Consider building a personal brand as a founder or owner — the source says that among their ecommerce clients, the ones whose results 'fly' typically have a celebrity or heavily involved, well-followed person associated with the company.

Understand the mechanism: personal brand is trust at scale, and trust matters most when a prospect is comparing your product with a competitor's; buyers assume a trusted founder has built the product carefully and cares about the category.
Weigh the barrier to entry as an advantage: building a personal brand takes time and resources, which the source argues deters competitors and produces a durable edge.

If a full personal brand is not viable, at minimum tell your origin story — the source's example is a mother who made a moisturiser for her child's eczema; that story is what made a friend of the presenter buy and then retell it to others.
Use the story in ad creative and copy, since it gives prospects a reason to choose and a reason to repeat the story to others.
caveats: The source acknowledges downsides: an attached personal brand makes an ecommerce business harder to sell later, though not impossible at large scale.
The claimed performance gap (a 2x versus 6x ROAS between otherwise similar businesses) is the presenter's anecdotal observation, not a controlled benchmark.
The source recommends external influencers as complementary, not as a substitute.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details Google Ads campaign strategies for e-commerce, covering campaign selection (Search and Shopping vs. Performance Max), product concentration, unit economics (AOV, LTV, margins), attribution tracking, and budget scaling. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, return on ad spend (ROAS), algorithm mechanics] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Structuring Google Ads campaigns for e-commerce brands by starting with intuitive Search and Shopping (text and product carousel) campaigns before layering in Performance Max once the account reaches a baseline volume of conversions (ideally 100+ purchases). Utilizing proper attribution and tracking tools (such as Hyros) to maintain clear visibility into cross-platform lead and purchase data. return on ad spend (ROAS) / Evaluating and managing e-commerce unit economics. Balancing Average Order Value (AOV), gross profit margins, and Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) to determine sustainable customer acquisition costs (CAC). Leveraging backend repeat purchases and high-LTV models (such as subscription or consumable ecosystems) to afford higher initial acquisition costs and enable aggressive campaign scaling. algorithm mechanics / Managing product catalog focus and algorithmic bidding. Avoiding fragmented ad spend across too many SKUs on cold traffic; instead, isolating winning product heroes to feed the Google Ads algorithm clean conversion data. Deploying broad product catalogs and remarketing dynamic product ads selectively to warm audiences who have already interacted with the site.

Look for. The recommended starting campaign types for e-commerce on Google Ads: Search and Shopping campaigns because they are intuitive and easy to manage before introducing automated Performance Max campaigns. The baseline conversion threshold for adding Performance Max: at least 100 purchases in the ad account to provide sufficient machine-learning data. The core principle of product focus for cold traffic: concentrating ad spend on a single or select few winning products rather than spreading budgets thinly across an entire catalog of SKUs.

Skip. Promotional pitches for agency management services or tracking software affiliate links.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.
